topic: Diagnosing illegal cancellation and lost-solution errors

traps.desc: divided both sides by sine, which throws away every angle where the sine is zero

problems.desc: Rubric for part (b): the response must say that dividing both sides by the sine is only legal when the sine is not zero, and that the two angles where it is zero are exactly the solutions destroyed by the division. A correct answer states the repair: move everything to one side and factor, so the sine survives as a factor rather than disappearing. Naming only that two answers are missing is partial credit.

traps.desc: took only the positive square root, dropping the whole negative case

problems.desc: Rubric for part (b): the response must say that a squared quantity equal to a positive number has two square roots, so the sine may be one half OR minus one half, and only the positive branch was taken. A correct answer notes that each branch supplies two angles in a full turn, so four solutions exist rather than two. Recommending the safer repair, factoring as a difference of squares, earns full credit.

traps.desc: cancelled a cosine from both sides, losing the two angles at which the cosine is zero

problems.desc: Rubric for part (b): the response must identify the cancelled cosine as the fault and say why the two right angles vanished. A correct answer explains that cancelling assumes the cosine is not zero, which is an assumption the problem never grants, and that factoring instead keeps both cases. Full credit requires naming the assumption, not merely listing the missing angles.

traps.desc: squared both sides and reported every root of the squared equation without testing them in the original

problems.desc: Rubric for part (b): the response must say that squaring both sides is not reversible, so it can create roots the original equation never had, and that every candidate therefore has to be substituted back. A correct answer performs that test on the false candidate and shows the two sides disagree there. Saying only that one answer is wrong, without the reason squaring produces it, is partial credit.

traps.desc: solved the doubled angle over the original interval instead of the doubled one, so half the solutions were never found

problems.desc: Rubric for part (b): the response must say that the doubled angle sweeps twice as far, so the interval for it runs to seven hundred and twenty degrees, and stopping at three hundred and sixty discards the second pass. A correct answer states the repair: substitute for the inside angle, multiply both endpoints of the interval by the coefficient, solve there, then divide every answer. Noting only that two answers are missing is partial credit.

traps.desc: cancelled the sine out of the double-angle term as well and lost the cosine factor with it

problems.desc: Rubric for part (c): the response must say that a common factor may be cancelled from a whole term, and that the second term is two times sine times cosine, so removing the sine leaves two cosine behind rather than a bare two. A correct answer writes the numerator as sine times the quantity one plus two cosine before dividing. Full credit requires naming the dropped cosine factor.

traps.desc: decided the factor giving a cosine of one had no solution and dropped it

problems.desc: Rubric for part (b): the response must say that a cosine of one is attainable and happens at zero degrees, which is inside the half-open interval, so that factor contributes a solution rather than none. A correct answer adds that the endpoint zero is included while three hundred and sixty is not, which is why the angle is listed once. Simply supplying the missing angle without saying why the student rejected it is partial credit.

traps.desc: cancelled the sine factor and also solved the doubled angle over the original interval, losing solutions twice over

problems.desc: Rubric for part (b): two independent faults must be named. First, dividing by the sine discards the angles where the sine is zero, namely zero and one hundred and eighty degrees. Second, the doubled angle needs an interval running to seven hundred and twenty degrees, and stopping early discards a further two angles. A correct answer says which missing solutions come from which fault; naming one fault only is half credit.
